summary:
Surface Signals is an interactive map for exploring real NISAR scene coverage at four study areas and anywhere else on the map. It searches NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for the provisional Level 2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) collection, then displays scene footprints, acquisition dates, ASF browse images, and links to the source products.

The map uses Esri World Imagery, with optional topographic/road and elevation-hillshade context layers. Drag or zoom to an area and choose Search this area to look up its NISAR passes. Choose a study site or a date window from 90 days through five years, or search all dates, to refresh the catalog results. Up to the 100 most recent scenes are shown per map extent. Select a footprint, timeline point, or scene to inspect the available browse images. When two or more passes are available, Compare passes opens a swipe comparison between their quicklooks; the play control animates chronologically through the timeline. Available polarimetric browse channels are called out for each selected pass. Site-specific radar context is presented as a hypothesis, not a measured change.

Enter and submit a city or region name to search OpenStreetMap; choose the matching result to set the map extent and load its NISAR passes.
details:
Surface Signals is an interactive web application that lets anyone explore real NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations of Earth’s surface.

Users can:

  • Search NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for provisional Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) scenes by map extent or by place name (city, region, landmark).
  • View scene footprints on satellite imagery, step through an observation timeline, and play chronological sequences.
  • Inspect ASF browse images, including available polarimetric channels, and compare two passes with a swipe view.
  • Open full products at the ASF DAAC.
  • Request Gemini-powered field notes, comparisons, explanations, and guided tours — always labeled as hypotheses, not measurements.

Four curated study areas (Amazon floodplain, Mississippi Delta, South Iceland, Jakarta basin) come with site-specific storytelling. A free-text place search (via OpenStreetMap Nominatim) opens the rest of the world. Time windows range from 90 days to five years, or “all dates” (up to 100 most recent scenes per view).

What benefits does it have?

  • Accessibility — Complex SAR data becomes explorable without downloading multi-gigabyte HDF5 files first.
  • Honesty about data maturity — Provisional products and AI outputs are clearly framed; browse images support exploration, not quantitative claims.
  • Real coverage, not demos — Live CMR search and ASF browse links, with D1 fallbacks for reliability.
  • Context for change — Polarizations, multi-date comparison, and physical-driver hypotheses help users ask better questions about wetlands, ice, coasts, and cities.
  • Open and deployable — Open-source stack on Cloudflare Workers, ready for educators, managers, and the public.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Help scientists, resource managers, educators, decision-makers, and the public see and discuss the patterns and rhythms of Earth’s surface using NISAR’s all-weather, day–night radar.

The goal is not to replace calibrated analysis, but to lower the barrier to discovery: find coverage, compare dates, understand what L-band can (and cannot) show, and connect visual differences to possible physical or human drivers — flooding under canopy, marsh–water edges, ice surface state, urban coastal change — with clear limits.

Longer term, the same pattern can support classroom modules, civic “my coast / my watershed” stories, and pathways into full product analysis.
